title: Christmas and Yule
when_text: 25 December; the twelve days run to Twelfth Night, 5 January, and Epiphany on 6 January
intro: Christmas falls just after the shortest days of the year, when the oldest tombs in the isles were built to catch the low midwinter sun. Its customs here are a mix of church services, royal ceremony, food and songs, and they were twice outlawed in the seventeenth century. Wales, Ireland and the Isle of Man keep customs of their own, from dawn carol services to a holiday for women.

facts.title: Midwinter sunrise inside Newgrange
facts.text: Newgrange in the Boyne valley is built so that the rising sun at the winter solstice shines through a slot over the entrance, the roofbox, and along the passage into the chamber. The light lasts about seventeen minutes; the first person in modern times to see it was the archaeologist Michael O'Kelly in 1967.

sources.title: Newgrange (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: This illumination lasts for approximately 17 minutes. Michael J. O'Kelly was the first person in modern times to observe this event on 21 December 1967.

facts.title: Maeshowe catches the midwinter sunset
facts.text: In Orkney the passage of the chambered tomb of Maeshowe faces the other way from Newgrange's: it lets in the light of the setting sun for a few days either side of the winter solstice, so that it reaches the back wall of the chamber.

sources.title: Maeshowe (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: lets the direct light of the setting sun into the chamber for a few days on each side of the winter solstice

facts.title: Bede's 'Mothers' night'
facts.text: The Northumbrian monk Bede wrote around 726 that the pagan English had called December and January the months of Yule, Giuli, and began their year on 25 December, a night they called Modranecht, 'Mothers' night'. It is the oldest account of a midwinter feast among the English; very little else is known about it.

sources.title: Yule (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Bede further writes that the heathen English started their year on 25 December, when Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus, and says that they called this Modranecht ("Mothers' night").

facts.title: A king crowned on Christmas Day
facts.text: William the Conqueror was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066, while the nave was still being built. The date copied the coronations of the Byzantine and Holy Roman emperors.

sources.title: Coronation of William the Conqueror (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The date chosen, Christmas Day, Monday 25 December, was in imitation of the customary date for the coronations of the eastern Byzantine emperors and the western Holy Roman emperors.

sources.title: Christmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: King William I of England was crowned on Christmas Day 1066.

facts.title: The thorn that flowers at Christmas
facts.text: The Glastonbury Thorn, a hawthorn that blooms in winter, is said in legend to have grown from the staff of Joseph of Arimathea. The thorn is first mentioned in a pamphlet of 1520, and a flowering sprig is still sent to the monarch every Christmas.

sources.title: Glastonbury Thorn (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the thorn is first mentioned in a pamphlet published by Richard Pynson in 1520

sources.title: Glastonbury Thorn (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A flowering sprig is sent to the British Monarch every Christmas.

facts.title: The first English carols
facts.text: The earliest Christmas carols written down in English are in a manuscript of about 1426 by John Awdlay, a chaplain at Haughmond Abbey in Shropshire. He recorded twenty-five 'caroles of Cristemas', probably sung by wassailers going from house to house.

sources.title: Christmas carol (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The earliest English Christmas carols appear in a 1426 manuscript by the Shropshire chaplain John Awdlay, who recorded twenty-five "caroles of Cristemas", likely sung by groups of wassailers traveling from house to house.

facts.title: Nine Lessons and Carols began in Cornwall
facts.text: The service of Nine Lessons and Carols is best known from King's College, Cambridge, which took it up in 1918, but it began at Truro, where Bishop Edward White Benson led the first one on Christmas Eve 1880, partly to keep men out of the pubs.

sources.title: Nine Lessons and Carols (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: conducted the first formal service of "Nine Lessons and Carols" on Christmas Eve (24 December) 1880. Benson, concerned at the excessive consumption of alcohol in Cornish pubs during the festive season

sources.title: Nine Lessons and Carols (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Notably in 1918, the Rev. Eric Milner-White the new dean of King's College, Cambridge, introduced the service to the college chapel

facts.title: Plygain: carols before dawn
facts.text: In Wales the plygain is a carol service held in church between three and six in the morning, traditionally on Christmas Day. It is thought to have replaced the Latin Mass at cockcrow after the Reformation. The carols, often of twenty verses or more, were traditionally sung only by men, and no carol may be sung twice in one service.

sources.title: Plygain (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Plygain is a traditional Welsh Christmas service which takes place in a church between three and six o'clock in the morning, traditionally on Christmas morning.

sources.title: Plygain (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The plygain service is thought to have been created to replace the traditional Latin pre-Reformation Mass at Cockcrow (missa in gallicantu).

sources.title: Plygain (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Traditionally the plygain carols were sung only by men.

sources.title: Plygain (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: often twenty or more verses

sources.title: Plygain (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: it is considered unacceptable to sing the same carol twice at the same service

facts.title: Scotland abolishes the Yule holiday
facts.text: After the Reformation the Kirk discouraged Christmas, and in 1640 the Scottish Parliament abolished the 'Yule vacation and all observation thereof'. Christmas Day only became a public holiday in Scotland in 1958, and Hogmanay was long the bigger winter celebration there.

sources.title: Christmas in Scotland (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A 1640 act of the Parliament of Scotland abolished the "Yule vacation and all observation thereof in time coming".

sources.title: Christmas in Scotland (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Christmas Day was made a public holiday in 1958 in Scotland, Boxing Day only in 1974. The New Year's Eve festivity, Hogmanay, was by far the largest celebration in Scotland.

facts.title: Christmas banned in England
facts.text: Parliament banned the celebration of Christmas in England in 1647. There were riots in its favour: for weeks Canterbury was held by rioters who hung holly on doorways and shouted royalist slogans. Christmas came back as a legal holiday with the Restoration in 1660.

sources.title: Christmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: for weeks Canterbury was controlled by the rioters, who decorated doorways with holly and shouted royalist slogans

sources.title: Christmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Christmas was restored as a legal holiday in England with the Restoration of King Charles II in 1660

facts.title: Mince pies once held meat
facts.text: Mince pies used to be filled with meat, such as ox tongue, beef or mutton, with spices and fruit. Cheap sugar from the West Indian plantations made them sweeter from the eighteenth century, and in the nineteenth recipes mostly dropped the meat, though the suet stayed.

sources.title: Mince pie (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The meat used in recipes varied, but included neat's tongue (cattle), beef, mutton, tripe and could also include fish.

sources.title: Mince pie (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The following century recipes increasingly stopped including meat

facts.title: Plum pudding without plums
facts.text: Christmas pudding is also called plum pudding, but 'plum' meant a raisin, and the pudding has no plums. The story that it goes back to a medieval custom of thirteen ingredients is a myth: recipes appear from the seventeenth century, one of the earliest in Mary Kettilby's book of 1714.

sources.title: Christmas pudding (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the pudding does not contain plums in the modern sense of the word

sources.title: Christmas pudding (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: One of the earliest plum pudding recipes is given by Mary Kettilby in her 1714 book

facts.title: Hunting the wren
facts.text: On St Stephen's Day, 26 December, groups in Ireland and the Isle of Man used to hunt a wren, the 'king of the birds', and carry it from house to house. A fake wren is used now; the Manx held a funeral for the bird and danced round a 'wren pole', and the wrenboys still parade in places such as Dingle.

sources.title: Wren Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: is an Irish and Manx custom on 26 December, Saint Stephen's Day

sources.title: Wren Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: On the Isle of Man, they held a funeral for the wren and danced around a 'wren pole'.

facts.title: Women's Christmas
facts.text: In Ireland 6 January, the last day of the Christmas season, is Nollaig na mBan, Women's Christmas. Traditionally the men did the housework that day to give the women a rest, and women still meet friends for a meal or a drink.

sources.title: Nollaig na mBan (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: men would take on what would have been seen as the traditional "female" household duties for the day, giving women the day off
